findings.vuln_type: Race condition / TOCTOU allows double redemption of gift cards
findings.why: The handler reads the gift card, checks status == ACTIVE, credits the store balance, and then marks the card redeemed as separate database operations with no transaction or row lock. The deployment uses multiple stateless replicas with a shared MySQL at REPEATABLE READ. Two concurrent requests with the same token can both read the card as ACTIVE (each in its own snapshot), both call CreditStoreCredit (committing double the face value), and then both call MarkGiftCardRedeemed. MarkGiftCardRedeemed also does not filter on status='ACTIVE' in its WHERE clause, so it provides no guard. This allows a gift card to be redeemed multiple times, inflating store credit.
findings.patch: Perform the status check, credit, and mark-redeemed inside a single transaction that locks the gift card row (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) and only credits if the card is still ACTIVE. Alternatively, make MarkGiftCardRedeemed conditional: UPDATE gift_card SET status='REDEEMED' ... WHERE id=? AND status='ACTIVE', check RowsAffected==1, and only call CreditStoreCredit if the update succeeded.

reasons.patch_quality: Đề xuất transaction với SELECT FOR UPDATE đáp ứng kiểm tra độc quyền, chỉ credit khi ACTIVE và commit cùng nhau; không thuộc patch_forbidden.

findings.vuln_type: Race condition / TOCTOU allows double-redeem of gift card
findings.why: The redeem flow reads the gift card status, checks it is ACTIVE, then credits the store balance and marks the card redeemed as two separate, non-atomic operations. MarkGiftCardRedeemed updates unconditionally (no `WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'`). findings.vuln_type: IDOR / Missing Cart Ownership Check
findings.why: redeem accepts dto.cartId from user input and passes it directly to carts.addDiscount without ever verifying that the cart belongs to ctx.user.id. claimReferral correctly calls carts.findOwnedOrFail(dto.cartId, ctx.user.id), but redeem does not. A customer can supply another customer's cartId and apply a promo discount to that victim's cart, or otherwise manipulate another user's cart.
findings.patch: Before proceeding with the promo lookup, call this.carts.findOwnedOrFail(dto.cartId, ctx.user.id) (as claimReferral does) to ensure the cart is owned by the authenticated user and is OPEN.

findings.vuln_type: TOCTOU Race Condition / Non-atomic Redemption
findings.why: redeem checks per-customer redemption (redemptions.count) and global budget (promo.redeemedCount >= promo.maxRedemptions) in separate SELECT queries, then performs an INSERT and an increment in separate statements with no transaction or locking. The deployment uses multiple stateless pods, so two concurrent requests from the same customer can both pass the checks and insert redemptions, allowing a customer to redeem the same promo more than once or exceed maxRedemptions. claimReferral correctly uses an atomic conditional UPDATE; redeem does not.
findings.patch: Wrap the check-and-insert in a transaction with row locking (e.g., SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the promo row), or enforce uniqueness via a database unique constraint on (promoId, customerId) and use an atomic conditional UPDATE for the global count (UPDATE promotion SET redeemedCount = redeemedCount + 1 WHERE id = :id AND redeemedCount < maxRedemptions), checking affected rows.

findings.vuln_type: TOCTOU race condition bypassing plan folder limit
findings.why: The create method checks the folder count against the plan entitlement using a non-locking read (entitlements.findByWorkspaceId and folders.countBySpaceIdAndDeletedFalse) under READ COMMITTED isolation with 4 instances and no session affinity. Two concurrent requests for the same space can both read the same count (e.g., 9 for a Free plan with a 10-folder ceiling), both pass the limit check, and both insert a folder, resulting in 11 folders — exceeding the plan limit and serving unpaid capacity. SpaceService.create correctly prevents the analogous race by calling entitlements.lockByWorkspaceId (PESSIMISTIC_WRITE), but FolderService.create does not acquire any lock before the count-check-insert sequence.
findings.patch: Acquire a pessimistic write lock on the entitlement (or an advisory lock keyed by spaceId/workspaceId) before counting folders, mirroring SpaceService.create. Replace entitlements.findByWorkspaceId with entitlements.lockByWorkspaceId(space.getWorkspaceId()) so that concurrent create transactions for the same workspace serialize on the entitlement row, ensuring the count-check-insert sequence is atomic with respect to other folder creations.

findings.vuln_type: Improper enforcement of one-reader-one-vote rule for comment reports
findings.why: The business rule states that a threshold of ten means ten distinct readers, and one reader objecting ten times counts as one opinion. However, InsertCommentReport performs a plain INSERT with no unique constraint or deduplication on (comment_id, reporter_id), and CountCommentReports uses COUNT(*) rather than COUNT(DISTINCT reporter_id). A single reader can call the report endpoint repeatedly, inserting multiple rows, and inflate the report count to meet the ReportsBeforeRemoval threshold, causing any comment to be pulled. The spam-flag path correctly uses INSERT IGNORE and COUNT(DISTINCT flagger_id), confirming the intended design.
findings.patch: Add a unique constraint on (comment_id, reporter_id) in the comment_report table, use INSERT IGNORE (or ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE) in InsertCommentReport, and change CountCommentReports to SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT reporter_id) FROM comment_report WHERE comment_id = ?. Alternatively, check for an existing report by the same user before inserting and return an error if already reported.

findings.vuln_type: Business logic flaw: single reader can inflate report count to pull any comment
findings.why: The business rule states the threshold represents the number of distinct readers objecting ('one reader objecting ten times is one reader's opinion'). findings.vuln_type: Information Exposure Through Returned Entity
findings.why: The list() method returns the raw Product entities directly (return { products: rows, ... }) without mapping through toPublicProductView(). The Product entity includes sensitive fields: costPriceCents and commissionBand (marketplace's private commercial contract terms with the seller), and suspensionPolicyCode, reviewerNotes, and sellerUnderInvestigation (internal trust-and-safety case-file data that shoppers must never see). The getForShopper() method correctly uses toPublicProductView() to strip these fields, but list() does not, leaking them to every caller including shoppers.
findings.patch: Map rows through toPublicProductView before returning: `return { products: rows.map(toPublicProductView), nextCursor: encodeCursor(rows) };` Note that nextCursor must be computed from the raw rows before mapping.

findings.vuln_type: Missing Role-Based Authorization on State Filter
findings.why: The list() endpoint accepts an arbitrary states[] parameter and applies it without checking the caller's role via ctx. A shopper can pass states=SUSPENDED (or DRAFT/INACTIVE) and retrieve non-public products. The spec states only LIVE products are part of the shop and that the seller-facing variant should show a seller 'their own listings in every state,' but there is no logic restricting shoppers to LIVE-only, nor any sellerId filter so a seller sees only their own products. Any role can enumerate all products in any state across all sellers.
findings.patch: Inside list(), enforce role-based constraints before applying dto.states: if ctx.role === 'shopper', force states to [LIVE] regardless of input; if ctx.role === 'seller', force a sellerId filter (p.sellerId = ctx.userId) and allow all states; only ts_reviewer should be permitted to pass arbitrary states without a sellerId filter.

findings.why: The `states` filter is taken directly from the client DTO (`dto.states`) and applied to the query without any server-side derivation from the caller's role. findings.vuln_type: Information disclosure to departed team members via stale participant list
findings.why: The business rule states that membership is continuous: the moment someone leaves a team they are outside the programme's confidence, including for reports filed while they were still on it. However, HandlePostComment sends comment bodies (which contain reproduction steps for unfixed defects) to every row in report_participant. That table is a static snapshot written at report-creation time and topped up when new people comment; it is never pruned when a team member leaves. As a result, a departed team member retains their report_participant row and continues to receive inline email notifications containing sensitive vulnerability details for reports they are no longer authorized to see. The weekly digest correctly uses ListCurrentTeamMembers (filtering on left_at IS NULL), but the per-comment notification path does not perform an equivalent current-membership check.
findings.patch: Before sending emails, filter the participant list against current team membership. For example, join report_participant to team_member (for the report's programme) with left_at IS NULL, or call ListCurrentTeamMembers and intersect the results with ListReportParticipants, so that only users who are still active team members (or the original researcher) receive the comment body. Alternatively, modify ListReportParticipants to join team_member and exclude rows where left_at IS NOT NULL.

HandleServeBlob looks up the blob solely by the user-supplied key and streams the content without ever checking that the caller's session belongs to blob.WorkspaceID. The blob key is a predictable-length identifier placed in ordinary browser-fetchable URLs that, per the application description, leak into browser history and copied page content. Card attachments hold sensitive workspace data (contracts, incident write-ups, customer exports), so any holder of a leaked key can download the file regardless of workspace membership. HandleServePreview has the identical defect.
findings.patch: Register /sp/attachment/blob and /sp/attachment/preview with scyna.WithScopes(shared.ROLE_MEMBER), and inside both handlers verify ctx.Session().WorkspaceID == blob.WorkspaceID before streaming; return Forbidden on mismatch. Alternatively, if keys must remain unauthenticated, make them unguessable signed tokens bound to the workspace and validated server-side.

findings.vuln_type: Improper Authentication — OTP sent to attacker-controlled number instead of listing's published number
findings.why: The claim flow is supposed to grant ownership to whoever can receive a call/SMS at the restaurant's published contact number (listing.ContactISD / listing.ContactPhone). However, HandleSendClaimOTP takes the ISD code and phone number from the request (request.GetIsdCode(), request.GetNumber()) and sends the OTP there without ever comparing them to the listing's stored contact number. An attacker can start a claim for any unclaimed listing, supply their own phone number, receive the OTP, verify it, and take ownership of the listing — including editing menus, prices, order history, and payout bank account.
findings.patch: After fetching the listing, validate that request.GetIsdCode() and request.GetNumber() match listing.ContactISD and listing.ContactPhone (normalized). Reject the request if they do not match. Do not accept a caller-supplied destination number for the claim OTP; always send to the listing's stored contact number.

findings.vuln_type: Missing email-confirmation check allows unconfirmed accounts to send platform-branded invitation emails with a spoofed inviter address
findings.why: The invite method sends an email from the platform's own domain that includes ctx.user.email as inviterEmail, but never checks ctx.user.emailConfirmedAt. The application description states that until an address is confirmed the platform only knows somebody typed it in, and the transfer method explicitly enforces confirmation for both parties—showing the control was intended. An attacker can register with a victim's email address, skip confirmation, and send platform-branded invitations that display the victim's email as the inviter, enabling phishing and impersonation through the platform's trusted domain.
findings.patch: Add a guard at the start of invite: if (!ctx.user.emailConfirmedAt) throw new ForbiddenException('confirm your email address first'); mirroring the check already present in transfer.

findings.vuln_type: Attacker-controlled name field in platform-sent email enables impersonation
findings.why: dto.name is user-supplied and used directly as inviterName in the email subject and body sent from the platform's own domain. An attacker can set name to a misleading value such as 'Platform Support' or 'Security Team'. The email subject becomes 'Platform Support invited you to …' and arrives from the platform's trusted sender, misleading recipients about who is actually inviting them. The inviter's real identity is only shown in the body via inviterEmail, which a casual reader may overlook.
findings.patch: Use the inviter's verified account display name (e.g., ctx.user.name) instead of the client-supplied dto.name, or validate that dto.name matches the authenticated user's profile name before sending.

findings.vuln_type: Business logic error — purchase overwrites existing seats instead of accumulating them
findings.why: When an organisation already holds a licence and places a new paid order, the code executes `existing.setSeats(order.getSeats())`, replacing the seat count with the new order's quantity rather than adding to it. The business rules state that seats bought at different times are covered for different lengths and that 'what the organisation ends up holding afterwards should be worth what it held before plus what it just paid for.' A repeat order for 1 seat on an organisation that already holds 10 seats silently discards 9 paid-for seats, causing loss of value the customer already purchased.
findings.patch: Replace `existing.setSeats(order.getSeats())` with `existing.setSeats(existing.getSeats() + order.getSeats())` so that new purchases accumulate onto existing entitlements.

findings.vuln_type: Business logic flaw: purchase replaces seat count instead of adding, violating the domain invariant that the organisation's holdings after a purchase should equal what it held before plus what it paid for
findings.why: The business specification states 'what the organisation ends up holding afterwards should be worth what it held before plus what it just paid for' and 'Seats bought at different times are covered for different lengths.' When an existing licence is found, the code does existing.setSeats(order.getSeats()), overwriting the seat count with the new order's quantity rather than adding to it. An org that already holds 100 seats and places a new order for 1 seat would end up with only 1 seat (while retaining the old expiry). This violates the core business invariant and can be exploited by any caller able to post an order (BILLING_SERVICE) to strip an organisation of paid-for seat coverage. The expiry date is only extended if the new purchase extends further, compounding the loss: seats are reduced but the date is not proportionally adjusted.
findings.patch: Replace existing.setSeats(order.getSeats()) with existing.setSeats(existing.getSeats() + order.getSeats()) so that purchased seats are additive, matching the business rule that holdings after a purchase equal prior holdings plus the new purchase.

findings.vuln_type: Mass assignment / privilege escalation via inherited CRUD patch
findings.why: ApiTokenController does not override patch, so CrudController.patch is reachable by any admin or owner. That method does Object.assign(row, body) with an unfiltered DeepPartial<ApiToken>, letting a caller set arbitrary entity fields—including roleIds. findings.vuln_type: Improper Authorization — fail-open default for unknown/legacy plan codes
findings.why: PLAN_FEATURES only contains free, pro, and business. The application description states that legacy plan codes (starter, plus, edu_2018, one-off enterprise codes) exist and are not backfilled in this table. findings.vuln_type: Insecure Direct Object Reference / PII Disclosure via non-secret order number
findings.why: The /sp/storefront/order/lookup-by-number endpoint is unauthenticated and requires only the order number, which the application description explicitly states is not a secret (warehouse staff read it aloud, customers paste it into chat, couriers quote it). The handler calls mysql.GetOrderByNumber with no additional verification factor (no email, no rate limiting) and returns the full Order struct — which includes recipient name, address lines, postcode, phone, email, card last four, and order lines. Anyone who knows or guesses an order number (format TEA-XXXX-XXXX, a small enumerable space) can retrieve another customer's complete PII. findings.vuln_type: IDOR / broken object authorization via non-secret order number
findings.why: The /sp/storefront/order/lookup-by-number endpoint is registered with no scopes (no authentication). It accepts only an order number, which the business context explicitly states is NOT a secret: it is printed on confirmation emails, packing slips, courier labels, read aloud by warehouse staff, pasted into chat, and quoted by couriers. Given only this non-secret identifier, the handler returns the full Order object (recipient name, address lines, postcode, phone, email, card last four, total) plus all order lines (items purchased). Any attacker who knows or guesses an order number can retrieve the PII and purchase details of any customer's order. The contrast with HandleTrackShipment — which requires both order number AND email and returns only tracking events — confirms that lookup-by-number is over-exposing data with an inadequate authorization factor.
findings.patch: Require the same two-factor verification used by HandleTrackShipment (order number + email) for lookup-by-number, or restrict the returned fields to only what the public tracking page needs (order status and tracking events). Do not return recipient name, address, phone, card last four, email, or item details from an unauthenticated endpoint keyed solely on a non-secret order number.

findings.vuln_type: Missing authorization on template project — information disclosure via template copy
findings.why: When useCustomTemplate is true, the service looks up a project by the user-supplied groupWithProjectTemplatesId and templateName, verifies only that it is marked as a template, and then copies all of its contents (repository, issues, snippets, merge requests) into the new project. There is no check that the calling user has read access to the template project. The application spec states a template's visibility and member list still apply and nominating a template 'is not a statement about who those people are.' A user who cannot read a PRIVATE or confidential template can still exfiltrate its full contents by supplying its group ID and name. ForkService correctly calls projectAccess.canRead before copying; ProjectCreateService omits the equivalent check.
findings.patch: After resolving the template project and before calling copier.copyInto, verify the caller's read access, e.g.: if (!projectAccess.canRead(principal.userId(), template)) { throw new NotFoundException("template not found"); }
